what_happened: Text written into docs/design/job-planning.md used the word "operator". A boundary test bans that word in Athena's files. Job a5sf was rejected because of it. The intervention log calls this the writer's own mistake. The word list the test scans for was not available to whoever wrote the text, and it was not run before the hand commit.
cause: The boundary rules live only in a test. Writers, whether the producer, the reader or a person making a hand commit, are not shown the banned words. Nothing runs the scan on the text before it is committed or handed to the verifier. A violation therefore shows up only when the full test suite runs and the job is rejected. The word "operator" is also the natural term for the person running Athena, so writers reach for it by default.
prevention: Expose the boundary scan as a single command that takes file paths or a diff. Run it automatically in the producer's pre-submit step and in a git pre-commit hook for hand commits. Include the banned-word list and the approved replacement terms in the producer's and reader's context. A violation then fails fast with the file, line and word, before the verifier runs.
proposed_request: Make the boundary test's banned-word scan runnable on its own against changed files, for example `athena check-boundary <paths>`. Run it automatically (1) before a producer submits its work, so a hit is fixed within the job, and (2) in a repo pre-commit hook, so hand commits are checked too. Put the banned-word list and the approved replacement terms into the producer's and reader's instructions. Done when: a docs edit containing a banned word such as "operator" is reported with file and line before the verifier runs, a clean edit passes, and the same word list is used by both the test and the command, with no second copy.
